traveler: Simon of Gitta, called Simon Magus, the Power That Is Called Great
title: The Silver and the Standing One: Simon of Samaria, the Offer at Sebaste, and the Fall on the Sacred Way
years: fl. c. 30-60 CE (birth and death unrecorded; the legendary deaths are set c. 64-68)
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Gitta, the village Justin names
stops.date_confidence: R. No first-century source gives Simon a birthplace. Justin Martyr, First Apology 26, written about a century later, calls him a Samaritan of the village called Gitto, and Justin was himself a Samaritan from Flavia Neapolis a few miles away, which is why he alone supplies the name. Gitta's site has never been identified, so the coordinate is the Nablus-area landmark and not a village. The year is an ordering device with no source behind it.
stops.campa: A village in Samaria that no excavation has found produces a man the Greek-writing world will argue about for three hundred years. Justin Martyr, born at Flavia Neapolis a short ride down the valley, is the only early writer who names the place, and he writes a full century after the events he is describing. Where Simon learned his art no source says. Acts, the earliest text of all, gives no village: only a man named Simon in the city, who had practiced magic there a long time.
suggested_refs: The unlocated site of Gitta, Samaria
Justin Martyr's own Samaritan origin at Flavia Neapolis

stops.name: Sebaste, the power that is called Great
stops.date_confidence: A for the episode, which is Acts 8:9-11. Acts names only the city of Samaria; the identification with the Herodian city of Sebaste is conventional and is R, and the coordinate is the Sebaste pin this corpus already uses. The year comes from the narrative sequence of Acts rather than from any datable event, and month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Before any Christian sets foot in the city, Simon is already the man everyone watches. He has practiced his art here a long time, Acts says, and he amazes the people of Samaria, saying that he is somebody great. The word it uses of him is mageuon, and it never describes a single thing he did with it. No source tells what he does to earn the title, either. The crowd answers him with one anyway, and the crowd is unanimous in it, from the least of them to the greatest.
stops.quote: This man is the power of God that is called Great.
suggested_refs: The Roman-era ruins of Sebaste at Sebastia

stops.name: Sebaste, baptized among the crowd
stops.date_confidence: A. Acts 8:5-13. The scene is attested to Acts and to nothing else; no second source anywhere records Simon's baptism, which is the single most awkward fact in his dossier for every later writer who needed him to be an unrepentant enemy. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Philip comes down to the city proclaiming the Messiah, and the crowd that had followed Simon follows Philip instead, watching unclean spirits come out with a loud cry and paralyzed people get up and walk. They are baptized, men and women together, in the name of Jesus Christ. Simon is baptized with them. Then he does the thing that no later summary of the episode ever quite explains: he stays. He attaches himself to Philip and goes nowhere, amazed at the signs and the great acts of power.
suggested_refs: jesus.journey.json, for the name in which the Samaritans are baptized

stops.name: Jerusalem, Peter and John sent down
stops.date_confidence: A for the sending, which is Acts 8:14-17. The Temple Mount coordinate is the canonical Jerusalem-apostolic pin already used in this corpus for the events of the thirties. Acts gives no date for any of it; the year follows its narrative sequence and month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The apostles in Jerusalem hear that Samaria has accepted the word of God, and they send Peter and John down to it. The Samaritans have been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, but the Spirit has come on none of them. The two apostles pray, and lay their hands on the baptized, and the Spirit is given. Acts does not describe what this looks like from outside. It says only that Simon sees it, and that what he sees is that the Spirit is given through the laying on of the apostles' hands.
sources: apostle_peter.journey.json, stop 'Sebaste, the man who offered money for the Spirit'
suggested_refs: The Jerusalem apostolic council that dispatches Peter and John to Samaria

stops.name: Sebaste, the money offered
stops.date_confidence: A. Acts 8:18-19, quoted verbatim. Nothing in the text characterizes the offer as made in secret or in bad faith; the reading of it as an attempt to buy a trade is an interpretation of what the verse says, and the file marks it as reading rather than as report. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He offers them money. The offer is the entire charge against him; nothing else in Acts is ever laid to his account. Nothing in the text says he offers it in secret, or in bad faith. He offers it the way a man buys a trade from the guild that holds it, having watched the work done and judged that he can do the work. What he asks for is not the Spirit but the transmission, the capacity to lay on hands and have the thing follow. He has believed, he has been baptized, and he has stayed with Philip.
stops.quote: Give me also this power so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.
suggested_refs: The word simony, formed from this transaction

stops.name: Sebaste, the gall of bitterness
stops.date_confidence: A. Acts 8:20-23, quoted verbatim. Peter's rebuke is the origin of the canonical category of simony, though the word itself is not coined for another five centuries; see the Rome stop dated 0590 for that. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Peter's answer is not a refusal but a curse, and it lands on the silver first and the man second. You have no part or share in this, he tells him, for your heart is not right before God. Repent of this wickedness of yours and pray to the Lord. Then he names what he sees standing in him, the gall of bitterness and the chains of wickedness. The rebuke is aimed at a baptized member of the congregation, not at an outsider, and it is a demand for repentance rather than a sentence. Nothing in Acts says whether Simon repents.
stops.quote: May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain God's gift with money!
suggested_refs: apostle_peter.journey.json, the same scene told from Peter's side

stops.name: Sebaste, the last words in the record
stops.date_confidence: A. Acts 8:24-25 is the end of the episode and the end of the secure record. Every subsequent stop in this file rests on sources written between eighty and three hundred years later, and each says so in its own field. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: He asks Peter to pray for him, that none of what has been said may come upon him. That is the last sentence Acts gives him, and everything else ever written about Simon is written into the silence after it. There is no expulsion, no death, no departure, no verdict on whether the prayer was made or answered. Peter and John go back toward Jerusalem, preaching in the Samaritan villages on the way, and the narrative leaves him standing in the city, baptized and rebuked and asking for intercession.
stops.quote: Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may happen to me.
suggested_refs: The absence of any death notice for Simon in Acts

stops.name: Gitta, Antonius and Rachel
stops.date_confidence: R, and late. The parents Antonius and Rachel appear only in the Pseudo-Clementine novels, at Recognitions 2.7 and Homilies 2.22, whose extant forms are fourth-century; the passages were not independently refetched for this file and are carried through the research pool's citation. No first- or second-century source names any relative of Simon at all. The date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Three centuries after Acts, a pair of Greek novels about Peter's travels hand Simon a family. His father is Antonius, his mother is Rachel, and his birthplace is the Gitta that Justin had named. Everything written earlier gives him no relative of any kind and no childhood; he arrives in the record already grown. The novels are fiction of a recognizable sort, romances built around long staged debates, and they are also the only place in the whole surviving literature where Simon has parents.
sources: Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions 2.7 and Homilies 2.22, via the research pool (not independently refetched)
Acts 8, Justin First Apology 26, and Irenaeus Against Heresies 1.23, for the absence
suggested_refs: The Pseudo-Clementine novels as the sole source for Simon's parentage

stops.name: Alexandria, the schools and the art
stops.date_confidence: R. The Pseudo-Clementine tradition sends Simon to Egypt to cultivate magic after a Greek literary education; the Alexandrian specification is a later refinement, and the passage could not be confirmed against the primary text in this research pass. Nothing in Acts, Justin, or Irenaeus places him in Egypt. The year orders the segment and is not a claim.
stops.campa: The novels send him to Egypt, where a man who wants the art goes to learn it. He is educated first in Greek letters and then in the thing that will be held against him for the rest of the record. The legend and the philology reach the same city by roads that never touch: M. David Litwa, working from the texts themselves, argues that the Simonian writings, the Great Declaration among them, are second-century compositions likely produced at Alexandria. Nothing in Acts, in Justin, or in Irenaeus puts Simon in Egypt at all.
sources: Pseudo-Clementine Homilies and Recognitions, as summarized in standard reference treatments
M. David Litwa, Simon of Samaria and the Simonians (2024), via secondary characterization; monograph not consulted
suggested_refs: Litwa's Alexandrian provenance argument for the Simonian literature

stops.name: Sebaste, Dositheus and the circle of thirty
stops.date_confidence: R, and novelistic. The Pseudo-Clementine narrative makes Simon one of thirty disciples of John the Baptist, has John die while Simon is in Egypt, gives the leadership to Dositheus, and then has Simon displace him. Helena is placed in the same circle. No place is specified, so the stop uses the Samaria pin. The date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: In the novels' version he belongs to the circle of thirty around John the Baptist, and while he is away in Egypt John dies and a man called Dositheus takes the leadership. Simon comes back, accepts second place, and then displaces him. Helena is in the circle too, one of the thirty, which is how the novels get her to his side without buying her. None of this is in Acts, or in Justin, or in Irenaeus. It first appears in a romance written three hundred years after the fact.
sources: Pseudo-Clementine Homilies and Recognitions, as characterized in standard reference summaries
suggested_refs: Dositheus of Samaria and the Baptist's circle in the Pseudo-Clementine tradition

stops.name: Tyre, redeemed from slavery
stops.date_confidence: R. Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.23, is the source for Tyre and for the purchase; Justin, First Apology 26, already knows a Helena travelling with Simon and calls her a former prostitute of Tyre. Both are hostile witnesses writing a century or more after the fact, and no independent source attests a historical Helena. The Tyre coordinate is the pin this corpus already uses for the city. The date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Irenaeus says he redeemed from slavery at Tyre, a city of Phoenicia, a certain woman named Helena, and that he carried her about with him afterwards. Justin, writing earlier, knows only that a woman of that name went around with him and had worked as a prostitute in the city. Everything else is doctrine. His followers call her the first idea generated by him, the Ennoia, the first conception of his mind, the mother of all, by whom he conceived the thought of forming angels and archangels.
stops.quote: this woman was the first conception of his mind, the mother of all, by whom, in the beginning, he conceived in his mind [the thought] of forming angels and archangels.
stops.quote_source: Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.23, ANF translation (newadvent.org/fathers/0103123.htm)
suggested_refs: Irenaeus's account of Helena as Ennoia, the fallen First Thought

stops.name: Tyre, the war fought on her account
stops.date_confidence: R. Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.23, for the transmigration and the identification with Helen of Troy, including the Stesichorus detail. This is Simonian doctrine as reported by an opponent writing about 180, not by anyone who held it. Whether a historical woman stands anywhere behind it cannot be established from the surviving sources, all of which are hostile. The date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The angels she made, in this telling, made the world, and then held her down inside it, passing her from body to body through the centuries so that she could not go back up. The woman a war was fought over ends in a brothel at Tyre, and a Samaritan buys her out of it. Irenaeus names one of the bodies: she was the Helen on whose account the Trojan War was undertaken, for whose sake also Stesichorus was struck blind, and then got his sight back by recanting the poem.
suggested_refs: The Stesichorus palinode, cited by Irenaeus inside the Simonian myth

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, where the pursuit begins
stops.date_confidence: R, and literary. The Pseudo-Clementine Homilies and Recognitions stage a running public disputation between Peter and Simon along the Phoenician coast; it is a narrative construction of the fourth-century novels, not a travel record. Caesarea opens the sequence at Homilies 1-3. The coordinate is the Caesarea pin this corpus already uses. Dates through this segment order the itinerary and nothing more.
stops.campa: The novels turn one encounter in Samaria into a chase the length of a coastline. It opens at Caesarea, where Peter is to debate him in public and Simon does not stay to be debated. For a figure whose only secure appearance is fifteen verses of one chapter of Acts, an entire itinerary is a strange thing to have acquired, invented so that he can go on losing arguments in new places. The pattern repeats at every city on the road north: the apostle arrives, the crowd assembles, the magician has already gone.
sources: apostle_peter.journey.json, for the corpus Caesarea pin
suggested_refs: The Pseudo-Clementine itinerary as a literary construction

stops.name: Tyre, gone before Peter lands
stops.date_confidence: R, literary. The Homilies place a stage of the pursuit at Tyre. The chapter text was not independently refetched for this stop, and the sequence is taken from the itinerary as it is described in standard reference treatments of the Pseudo-Clementines. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Peter follows him north to Tyre. The novels give the city a crowd, a disputation, and Simon's absence from it, because he has taken his companions on to the next port before the apostle's ship is in. The Homilies are careful about the order of the stops, which is how the itinerary survives at all as a list of names in a fixed sequence. What they are not careful about is whether any of it happened, a question they never raise, because the debate is the point and the coast is only the corridor it runs down.
sources: Pseudo-Clementine Homilies, narrative geography (Ante-Nicene Fathers, newadvent.org)
suggested_refs: The Phoenician coast road between Caesarea and Antioch

stops.name: Sidon, the apostle behind the magician
stops.date_confidence: R, literary, and unconfirmed against the primary chapter text in this research pass. Sidon appears in the Pseudo-Clementine itinerary between Tyre and Berytus. The coordinate is the corpus Sidon pin. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Sidon, next along the coast road, between Tyre and Berytus in the itinerary. Peter preaches, and the record of what Simon does here is that he has left. The Homilies move their two figures up the Phoenician shore in fixed order, apostle behind magician, each city a stage set for a doctrinal contest that keeps failing to take place. The cities are furniture. The geography is real and the road can still be walked, and the men walking it are characters in a fourth-century book about a first-century argument.
sources: Pseudo-Clementine Homilies, narrative geography (Ante-Nicene Fathers, newadvent.org)
suggested_refs: Sidon in the Pseudo-Clementine pursuit sequence

stops.name: Berytus, one harbor ahead
stops.date_confidence: R, literary. Homilies 7 supplies the flight to Berytus and Simon's failure to wait even a day; the quoted phrasing is from the Ante-Nicene Fathers translation at newadvent.org/fathers/080807.htm. It is a novel, and the detail's reportorial texture is a novelist's effect. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: At Berytus the novels give a detail with the texture of reporting. The magician is always one harbor ahead, and the book keeps this up for a dozen more sections, producing the odd effect of a fugitive whose route is better documented than his existence. Here is how it sounds. When Simon heard that Peter was coming, the Homilies say, he straightway fled to Beyrout, and when Peter came there he learned that Simon had not waited for them for a day but had gone straightway on.
suggested_refs: Homilies 7, the Berytus flight

stops.name: Byblus, the stop the summaries lose
stops.date_confidence: R, literary. Homilies 7 places Byblus between Berytus and Tripolis; most summaries of the Pseudo-Clementine itinerary omit it and run Berytus straight into Tripolis, which is the error this stop exists to correct. The coordinate is the modern town of Jbeil. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Byblus falls between Berytus and Tripolis in the Homilies, and it falls out of nearly every summary of the route, which jump from the one to the other and lose it. Peter arrives; Simon has gone on ahead of him again, as he has at every harbor since Caesarea. The novels use the town as a waypoint, one line in a chase. It is older than everything else in the itinerary by two thousand years, older than the alphabet that carries its name, a port that was shipping cedar to Egypt before either of these men had a religion to argue about.
suggested_refs: Byblus (Jbeil), routinely dropped from summaries of the Pseudo-Clementine route

stops.name: Tripolis, the pretext that keeps the apostle moving
stops.date_confidence: R, literary, and unconfirmed against the primary chapter text in this research pass. Tripolis occupies Homilies 8-11, where Peter teaches and baptizes at length and Simon is absent. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Tripolis holds Peter for four books of the Homilies, teaching and baptizing while the man he came for is somewhere else entirely. The pursuit has by now stopped being a pursuit and become a circuit of instruction, with Simon serving as the reason for the journey rather than as a participant in it. He is the pretext that keeps the apostle moving up the coast, and across four books of instruction, baptisms, and household teaching he does not once appear on the page. The reader is told repeatedly that he is near.
sources: Pseudo-Clementine Homilies 8-11, narrative geography (Ante-Nicene Fathers, newadvent.org)
suggested_refs: The Tripolis instruction sequence in the Homilies

stops.name: Laodicea, the long disputation
stops.date_confidence: R, literary. Homilies 12-20 stage the extended disputation at Laodicea, the debate the whole chase has been arranging. The substance attributed to Simon there, that the God of the Law is not the highest God, is reported entirely by his opponents and is not independently attested. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: At Laodicea the chase finally stops running and the two men are put in a room together for the long disputation the whole book has been arranging, nine books of it. Simon argues that the God of the Law is not the highest God, and that the scriptures contain false passages that must be sifted. He loses, at length, in a text composed entirely by his opponents. It is the fullest account anywhere of what a Simonian is supposed to have believed, and whether any Simonian ever said it cannot be settled from anything that survives. Then he leaves for Antioch.
sources: Pseudo-Clementine Homilies 12-20, narrative geography (Ante-Nicene Fathers, newadvent.org)
suggested_refs: The Laodicea disputation, Homilies 16-19

stops.name: Antioch, the one city that can be checked
stops.date_confidence: R for the Pseudo-Clementine ending of the itinerary at Antioch; A for Justin's separate and much earlier report that Menander of Capparetaea taught there. Justin, writing about 150, says he had met elderly followers. The coordinate is the Antioch pin this corpus already uses. The date orders the segment and does not date Menander, whose floruit is unknown.
stops.campa: Antioch closes the itinerary, and it is also the one city on the list where something outside the novels can be checked. Justin Martyr, who had met elderly followers of the movement, reports that a Samaritan named Menander, from the village of Capparetaea, set up as a teacher in this city and told his disciples they would not die. Whatever the novels are doing with Antioch, somebody was in fact teaching Simonian doctrine in it, within living memory of people Justin talked to.
sources: Pseudo-Clementine Homilies and Recognitions, for the itinerary's end
suggested_refs: Menander of Capparetaea and the Simonian school at Antioch

stops.name: Rome, mighty acts by the art of demons
stops.date_confidence: R. Justin Martyr, First Apology 26, is the earliest source placing Simon in Rome, writing about 150 and dating the visit to the reign of Claudius, 41 to 54. No Roman historian, inscription, rescript, or trial record corroborates any of it, and every later report descends from Justin. The Rome coordinate is the corpus pin. The year sits inside Claudius's reign and is otherwise an ordering device.
stops.campa: Justin tells the emperor Antoninus Pius, in a document meant to be read at court, that a Samaritan from the village of Gitto came to Rome under Claudius and did mighty acts of magic by the art of the devils operating in him. Eusebius will quote the passage in full a century and a half later, and that is the channel through which most of the Middle Ages receives it. Outside the Christian apologists, no Roman source of any kind, official or literary, records that such a man was ever in the city.
stops.quote: There was a Samaritan, Simon, a native of the village called Gitto, who in the reign of Claudius Caesar, and in your royal city of Rome, did mighty acts of magic, by virtue of the art of the devils operating in him.
stops.quote_source: Justin Martyr, First Apology 26, ANF translation (newadvent.org/fathers/0126.htm)
sources: apostle_peter.journey.json, stop 'Rome, the arrival nobody can date'
suggested_refs: The complete absence of Roman documentary corroboration for Simon in the capital

stops.name: The Tiber, between the two bridges
stops.date_confidence: R, and later positively explained away. Justin, First Apology 26, says the statue stood on the river Tiber, between the two bridges; he does not say Tiber Island, which is the standard modern inference from the Pons Fabricius and the Pons Cestius. The coordinate follows that inference and is labelled as inference. What was actually excavated on the island in July 1574 is a base inscribed to the Sabine god Semo Sancus; see the stop dated 1574.
stops.campa: He goes further than a report of magic. He tells the emperor that Rome honored the man as a god, put up a statue to him on the Tiber between the two bridges, and cut a Latin inscription into it. Justin adds that almost all Samaritans, and a few of other nations, worship Simon as the first God, and Helena beside him as the first idea generated by him. He is a Samaritan writing to Romans about a Roman monument, and he expects the court to be able to walk down and look at it.
stops.quote_source: Justin Martyr, First Apology 26, the inscription he reports, rendered by him as 'To Simon the holy God'
suggested_refs: The Pons Fabricius and the Pons Cestius, the two bridges of Justin's phrase

stops.name: Caesarea Maritima, the magician in Felix's household
stops.date_confidence: A for the passage, R for the identification. Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 20.142, describes a Jewish magician from Cyprus in the service of the procurator Felix in the early fifties. The critical Greek text names him Atomos; the Latin version and the Epitome read Simon, which is what Whiston's English translation prints. The identification with Simon Magus, proposed by Hans Waitz and others, is a disputed minority hypothesis, and the ethnicity does not match.
stops.campa: In Josephus a magician attached to the procurator Felix is sent to Drusilla, the Jewish king's daughter, to talk her into leaving her husband Azizus and marrying the Roman. He succeeds. The Greek manuscripts call this man Atomos; the Latin ones call him Simon, and the standard English translation follows the Latin. On that single variant a small line of scholars, Hans Waitz among them, has tried to put Simon Magus inside a procurator's household. The case has never carried. He is a Cypriot Jew in Josephus, not a Samaritan.
sources: Hans Waitz's identification, as reported in standard reference treatments
suggested_refs: The Atomos/Simon variant between the Greek text and the Latin version of Antiquities 20.142

stops.name: Sebaste, Son, Father, and Spirit
stops.date_confidence: A for what Irenaeus reports, R for whether Simon taught it. Against Heresies 1.23, written about 180, is the source; it is a hostile catalogue of heresies and its author never met a Simonian. Irenaeus gives no place for the teaching, so the stop sits at the Samaria pin. The year is an ordering device inside the conventional lifetime.
stops.campa: The doctrine, as his opponents set it down, is one power wearing three faces across three peoples. He appeared among the Jews as the Son, writes Irenaeus, who records it in order to destroy it, but descended in Samaria as the Father, while he came to the other nations in the character of the Holy Spirit. It is an answer to a real question: how does one God come to be met under different names by different nations? The man giving the answer says the God in question is himself.
stops.quote: This man, then, was glorified by many as if he were a god; and he taught that it was himself who appeared among the Jews as the Son, but descended in Samaria as the Father, while he came to other nations in the character of the Holy Spirit.
stops.quote_source: Irenaeus, Against Heresies I.23, ANF translation (newadvent.org/fathers/0103123.htm)
suggested_refs: The heresiological catalogue as the only vehicle for Simonian doctrine

stops.name: Sebaste, the boundless power and the six roots
stops.date_confidence: R. The Refutation of All Heresies, book 6, traditionally ascribed to Hippolytus, quotes at length from a text it calls the Great Declaration, the Apophasis Megale, and attributes it to Simon. Modern scholarship generally dates that text to the second century and to his school rather than to him, so the quoted formula is not a secure autograph of the historical Simon. No place is given, so the stop sits at the Samaria pin. The date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The Refutation quotes a book. In it an infinite Boundless Power is likened to fire, which has a visible part and a hidden one, and out of it come six roots in three pairs, male and female together: Mind and Thought, Voice and Name, Reason and Reflection. The system is close enough to later Gnostic cosmology that the heresiologists made Simon the head of the whole family, and far enough from Acts that the man in Acts is unrecognizable inside it. Above the roots and through them, says the book, is the one who stood, stands, and will stand.
stops.quote_source: Refutation of All Heresies VI, quoting the Simonian Apophasis Megale (newadvent.org/fathers/050106.htm)
sources: Refutation of All Heresies 6.9-18, attributed to Hippolytus (newadvent.org/fathers/050106.htm)
suggested_refs: The Apophasis Megale, surviving only inside the text that refutes it

stops.name: Antioch, the chain begins
stops.date_confidence: A for Menander's existence and teaching, from Justin, First Apology 26, and Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.23; R for his personal discipleship under Simon, which is attested only by hostile sources building a succession. Menander's dates are unknown; the year is an ordering device. The coordinate is the corpus Antioch pin.
stops.campa: Menander is a Samaritan too, out of Capparetaea, and he teaches at Antioch that those he baptizes will not die but will hold an immortal youth in this life. Justin has met people who followed him, so the man himself is not in doubt; the genealogy that follows is the invention. Irenaeus takes the two and makes them the first links in a chain, and every later heresiologist lengthens it, until by the fourth century every doctrine the church has condemned descends from a man who once offered two apostles money in Samaria.
suggested_refs: The heresiological succession Simon to Menander to Saturninus and Basilides

stops.name: Aricia, the senator and the emptied church
stops.date_confidence: R, apocryphal. The Acts of Peter, composed in Greek in the later second century, probably in Asia Minor, and surviving mainly in the Latin Vercelli manuscript, stages the Roman contest after Paul departs for Spain. It is legend, not record, and its Neronian setting is dramatic rather than dated. Dates through this segment order the scenes only.
stops.campa: In the Acts of Peter the apostle Paul has sailed for Spain and left the Roman congregation without him, and into that gap comes Simon, working from Aricia in the Alban hills. He takes the senator Marcellus, a rich man who had built a house for the poor out of his own money and now spends it on the magician instead. The church in the city collapses down to a handful. Peter is sent for from Jerusalem to repair what one man has undone in a few months.
sources: apostle_paul.journey.json, for the departure that opens the gap
suggested_refs: The Vercelli Codex, sole substantial witness to the Acts of Peter

stops.name: Rome, the house of Marcellus and the dog
stops.date_confidence: R, apocryphal. Acts of Peter, the summoning at the house of Marcellus. The coordinate is a Roman Forum area pin for a house the text does not locate precisely. The scene is legend of the late second century and has no historical standing whatever; it is included because it is the form in which the contest actually reached medieval Europe.
stops.campa: Peter comes to Marcellus's door and Simon will not come out to him. There is a great dog chained at the entrance. Peter looses it and gives it a message to carry, and the dog goes in on its hind legs and speaks the message aloud in front of the whole household. Simon hears his summons delivered by an animal. The dog comes back out, lies down at the apostle's feet, and dies there, and Marcellus throws himself into the street and asks to be taken back.
stops.quote: Peter the servant of Christ who standeth at the door saith unto thee: Come forth abroad
stops.quote_source: Acts of Peter (Vercelli Acts), the dog's message at the house of Marcellus
suggested_refs: The speaking dog of the Acts of Peter

stops.name: Rome, Via Sacra: the boast
stops.date_confidence: R, apocryphal. Acts of Peter, chapters XXXI-XXXII. The flight is the earliest extant version of the Simon death tradition and is absent from Acts, from Justin, and from Irenaeus, all three of whom had every polemical reason to use it if they had known it. The Via Sacra coordinate follows the text's own setting near the Forum. The date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Beaten in every contest the book has staged for him, Simon announces the last one himself. Tomorrow he will forsake the Romans, godless and impious as they are, and fly up to God whose Power he is. A crowd gathers on the Sacred Way in the morning to watch him do it. He rises over the city, over the temples and the hills, and the people who had come back to Peter turn and look up, and some of them start to doubt, because the impossible thing is happening above the Forum.
stops.quote: to-morrow I shall forsake you, godless and impious that ye are, and fly up unto God whose Power I am
stops.quote_source: Acts of Peter (Vercelli Acts), ch. XXXI-XXXII
suggested_refs: The flight over Rome, absent from every source earlier than c. 180

stops.name: Rome, Via Sacra: the leg broken in three places
stops.date_confidence: R, apocryphal. Acts of Peter, ch. XXXII. Peter's prayer in the text asks specifically that Simon be disabled rather than killed. The same text is the earliest extant source for Peter's own crucifixion head downward, which is worth stating plainly: the two most famous scenes in the Petrine legend stand on exactly the same evidentiary footing. The date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Peter does not pray that he be killed. He prays that he be brought down and disabled and left alive and broken. This is the earliest surviving version of the death, and it comes out of the same book, in the same few pages, that gives the world Peter crucified upside down. Simon falls onto the Sacred Way with his leg broken in three places, and the crowd that had been looking up a moment earlier picks up stones, and finishes what the fall began, and goes home.
stops.quote: And he fell from the height and brake his leg in three places. Then every man cast stones at him and went away home
stops.quote_source: Acts of Peter (Vercelli Acts), ch. XXXII
suggested_refs: The basalt stones in the south transept of Santa Francesca Romana, Rome, said by local tradition to bear the knee-prints Peter left praying against this flight (41.8912, 12.4889); Peter's object, not Simon's

stops.name: Aricia, carried out in the dark
stops.date_confidence: R, apocryphal. Acts of Peter. The text has Simon survive the fall and be moved by night to Aricia, the place he had been operating from before Peter arrived, and then moved on again. The date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: He is not dead. Somebody lifts the broken man out of the city in the dark and carries him back to Aricia, which is where he had been working from before the apostle arrived. The Acts of Peter, having spent thirty chapters building the contest up, gives the aftermath a few lines and no scene at all, as though the story that has been telling him had finished with him. He stays there a while with the leg unset. Then he is moved again, further south along the coast.
suggested_refs: Aricia (Ariccia) in the Alban hills, the Acts of Peter's staging ground

stops.name: Terracina, the two physicians
stops.date_confidence: R, apocryphal. Acts of Peter: Simon is brought to Terracina, to one Castor, and is sorely cut by two physicians, and dies of it. This is one of four incompatible deaths in the tradition; see the two stops that follow, and note that Acts 8 reports no death at all. The date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: The last stage is Terracina, in the house of a man called Castor, where two physicians work on the shattered leg and Simon dies under their hands. The text says only that he was sorely cut by them, and gives no last words. The Acts of Peter puts him there and stops. A man who had claimed to be the standing power of God, the one who stood and stands and will stand, ends on a table in a coastal town in Latium, in a house belonging to somebody nobody has heard of, killed by surgery.
suggested_refs: Terracina and the house of Castor, the Acts of Peter's death scene

stops.name: Rome, the trench and the third day
stops.date_confidence: R, and a competing tradition that cannot be reconciled with the one above. The Refutation of All Heresies, book 6, has Simon order his disciples to bury him alive, promising to rise on the third day, and he does not rise. The place is not recoverable: the ANF text carries a manuscript lacuna exactly there, reading 'This man, ultimately repairing to ... (and) sitting under a plane tree'. The preceding narrative has him at Rome, so the stop uses the Rome pin. The Catholic Encyclopedia's supplement of Gitta is editorial, not Hippolytus's word.
stops.campa: A different book kills him a different way. In the Refutation he has lost his following, and sitting under a plane tree he tells his disciples to dig a trench and bury him alive in it, promising to come out on the third day. They do it. Where the tree stood the manuscript cannot say: the sentence breaks off in the middle at exactly that word, and the place is a hole in the parchment. About what came afterward the text is not uncertain at all. He remained in that grave until this day, for he was not the Christ.
sources: Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Simon Magus' (newadvent.org/cathen/13797b.htm), for the editorial supplement
suggested_refs: The lacuna in the Refutation at the place-name of Simon's burial

stops.name: Rome, the tower before Nero
stops.date_confidence: R, and flagged as unverified. The Acts of Peter and Paul, a text distinct from and later than the Acts of Peter, stages the flight from a wooden tower before Nero, with the body falling in four parts and Nero keeping the corpse three days to test the promised resurrection. The research for this file could not confirm the episode against a primary or reliably excerpted text and recommended it be treated as unverified. It is kept, with that failure stated here, rather than silently dropped. The coordinate is a general Rome pin for an unspecified imperial setting.
stops.campa: A later book rebuilds the whole scene with an emperor inside it. Nero has Simon at court; a wooden tower is put up on the emperor's order; he goes off it, and Peter tells the spirits holding him up to let go. The body comes apart into four pieces on the ground. Nero, who had believed him, keeps the remains under guard for three days, waiting for the resurrection he was promised. Nothing happens on the third day, and the emperor turns on the apostles instead.
sources: Acts of Peter and Paul, as reported in standard reference treatments of the Simon-Peter legend cycle; primary text not confirmed in this research pass
suggested_refs: The four incompatible deaths of Simon Magus, none of them in Acts

stops.name: Jerusalem, told to the catechumens
stops.date_confidence: A for the text, R for its content. Cyril of Jerusalem's Catechetical Lecture 6 carries the story. The lectures were delivered around 350, or perhaps 348 while Cyril was still a priest deputising for his bishop; the commonly quoted range of 346 to 348 is not the standard one and is not used here. Cyril has Claudius himself erect the statue, which goes beyond Justin. The coordinate is the Holy Sepulchre precinct.
stops.campa: Three centuries on, a bishop instructing people who are preparing for baptism uses Simon as the cautionary example, and by now the story has grown a chariot. He promised to rise aloft to heaven, Cyril says, and came riding in a demon's chariot on the air. In this version it takes both apostles to bring him down, Peter and Paul praying in concert, and Claudius himself is the one who set up the statue on the Tiber, which is more than Justin ever claimed. The people hearing it are a few weeks away from their own baptism.
suggested_refs: Cyril's demon-drawn chariot, a mechanism absent from the Acts of Peter

stops.name: Sebaste, the sect almost extinct
stops.date_confidence: A for Epiphanius, whose Panarion was written about 375 to 377 and describes the Simonians as almost extinct. R for the Origen report, that their number was already very small in the mid-third century: that citation was not independently refetched in this research pass and is carried from the pool. The Samaria pin stands for the region where the sect is placed. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Epiphanius of Salamis, cataloguing every heresy he can find for the Panarion, puts the Simonians near the head of his list and then reports that they are by now almost extinct. Origen had said something similar a century earlier, that the number of Simonians was very small. The doctrine the heresiologists had made the source of everything they hated had, by the time they finished describing it, almost nobody left holding it anywhere. The name went on without the people. Epiphanius was writing between about 375 and 377.
sources: Origen, as reported in the research pool (not independently refetched)
suggested_refs: The Panarion's placement of the Simonians at the head of the heresies

stops.name: Rome, the sin that takes his name
stops.date_confidence: A. Simony, the buying or selling of ecclesiastical office, sacraments, or spiritual things, is named from Acts 8; Gregory I, pope from 590 to 604, is credited with putting the phrase simoniac heresy into ecclesiastical use, and conciliar prohibitions go back to the Synod of Elvira about 305 and to Nicaea in 325. The date marks Gregory's accession. The Dante quotation is Longfellow's translation of Inferno XIX; the wording carried by the research pool matched no standard translation and is not used.
stops.campa: The transaction he proposed in Samaria becomes a legal category. Councils prohibit the practice at Elvira and at Nicaea before anyone attaches his name to it; Gregory the Great fixes the name, and simony enters canon law as a heresy rather than as an abuse. Dante puts him at the head of the third pouch of the eighth circle and addresses him directly, by name, in the canto's first line, before describing anything at all, and then fills the pouch with popes planted head down in the rock with their feet on fire.
stops.quote: O Simon Magus, and his wretched followers, / Rapacious ones, who the things of God, / Which ought to be the brides of Righteousness, / Prostitute for the gold and silver bright!
stops.quote_source: Dante, Inferno XIX.1-4, Longfellow translation (Project Gutenberg #1001)
suggested_refs: The third bolgia of the eighth circle, reserved for the sin named after him

stops.name: Kerry, the druid's associate
stops.date_confidence: R, and the coordinate is borrowed. English Wikipedia, 'Simon Magus', states that Simon is said to have come to the aid of the druid Mog Ruith, which reverses the more commonly retold version in which Mog Ruith is Simon's pupil and builds his flying machine. The article names no place at all: the Valentia Island coordinate comes from Mog Ruith's own separate tradition and is not attested for this legend. Nothing here claims Simon travelled to Ireland. The date is an ordering device for the medieval Irish material.
stops.campa: Latin magus covers both the magician and the druid, and on that one word the Christian arch-magician is naturalized into Irish learned tradition. He turns up in the orbit of Mog Ruith, the blind druid of Kerry, coming to that druid's aid. The version more often retold sends the traffic the other way and makes Mog Ruith the student, the one who builds Simon's flying machine. Which direction the medieval Irish material actually ran is not settled by anything in it. No source claims Simon ever went to Ireland; what is claimed is a working relationship.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Simon Magus', on the Mog Ruith connection
suggested_refs: Mog Ruith in the medieval Irish tradition, and the ambiguity of Latin magus

stops.name: Toulouse, Saint-Sernin: the fall cut in stone
stops.date_confidence: A for the sculpture, R for its date. A Simon Magus relief at the gate of the Basilica of Saint-Sernin is documented, and the basilica's own sculpture inventory carries Simon the magician with demons alongside a birth of the vine. The building campaign runs through the late eleventh and early twelfth centuries; the altar was consecrated by Urban II on 24 May 1096 and work continued past 1120. The date given is the consecration and stands for the campaign. The coordinate is the corpus Saint-Sernin pin.
stops.campa: On the pilgrimage road to Compostela the fall goes into stone. A relief at the gate of Saint-Sernin shows the magician, and the basilica's inventory of sculpture carries a Simon the magician with his demons, set beside a birth of the vine. The people walking to Santiago do not read Irenaeus and have never heard of the Apophasis Megale. They read the porch, and what the porch tells them is that a man once flew over Rome and was brought down out of the air by prayer.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Simon Magus' (image caption for the Saint-Sernin relief)
suggested_refs: The Romanesque sculptural program of Saint-Sernin on the road to Compostela

stops.name: Rome, the Capitol in the Golden Legend
stops.date_confidence: R, a medieval synthesis. Jacobus de Voragine's Golden Legend, compiled in the 1260s, gathers the late-antique versions into the life of Saints Peter and Paul: the tower on the Capitol, the flight before Nero, the demons commanded to release him, the fall, the broken neck. The specific chapter text was not independently retrieved for this file. Site and injury both differ from the Acts of Peter, which has the Via Sacra and a leg broken in three places, and the two are not reconciled here.
stops.campa: Jacobus de Voragine collects the versions and issues the one that Western Europe will actually know. In his telling Simon climbs a high tower on the Capitol in front of Nero, announces that he is going up to heaven, and gets off the ground. Peter orders the demons carrying him to let go their hold. He falls and breaks his neck. The Via Sacra is gone, the two physicians at Terracina are gone, the stoning is gone, and what survives into four centuries of altarpieces is this.
sources: Jacobus de Voragine, Golden Legend, Lives of Peter and Paul (chapter text not independently retrieved)
suggested_refs: The Golden Legend's Capitoline tower, displacing the Acts of Peter's Via Sacra

stops.name: Florence, the Brancacci wall
stops.date_confidence: A. Filippino Lippi completes Masaccio's unfinished decoration of the Brancacci Chapel in Santa Maria del Carmine; the Disputation with Simon Magus before Nero and the Crucifixion of Saint Peter belong to that campaign, conventionally dated about 1482 to 1485, and the date given is the end of it. The research pool carried a narrower and earlier 1481 to 1482 in one lens and the correct range in another; the correct range is used. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: Filippino Lippi finishes what Masaccio left, and on one wall he puts the dispute and its consequence into a single continuous space: Simon arguing before Nero at one end, Peter hanging head downward at the other, the same crowd standing for both. The contest and the martyrdom stop being two episodes with a gap between them and become one room, with the Florentines who commissioned it standing inside it. Among the onlookers Lippi paints himself, and Antonio del Pollaiuolo, and Botticelli, watching from within the picture.
suggested_refs: Filippino Lippi's Disputation with Simon Magus and Crucifixion of St Peter, Brancacci Chapel

stops.name: Tiber Island, the stone dug up
stops.date_confidence: A. A marble base was excavated on Tiber Island in July 1574, near the site of the temple of Iupiter Iurarius, inscribed SEMONI SANCO DEO FIDIO SACRVM, to the Sabine deity Semo Sancus Dius Fidius; it is CIL VI.567 and is now in the Vatican's Galleria Lapidaria. The wording and findspot match Justin's description closely enough that misreading is the standard scholarly explanation of his claim. It does not by itself disprove that Simon was ever in Rome. Day is a placeholder within the month.
stops.campa: Fourteen hundred years after Justin, workmen on the island turn up the stone. It is a dedication to Semo Sancus Dius Fidius, an old Sabine god of oaths and sworn treaties, and the letters run SEMONI SANCO DEO FIDIO SACRVM. Justin had read, or had been told by someone else, Simoni Deo Sancto. One monument, two gods, and the entire documentary basis for a Roman cult of Simon Magus turns out to be a Samaritan apologist misconstruing a Latin dative on a riverbank.
sources: Platner and Ashby, Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome, s.v. Semo Sancus (penelope.uchicago.edu)
suggested_refs: CIL VI.567, Vatican Galleria Lapidaria

stops.name: Vatican, the mosaic never made
stops.date_confidence: A for the commission history. Pompeo Batoni designed a Fall of Simon Magus in 1746 for an altarpiece in St Peter's Basilica intended to be translated into mosaic because of damage from humidity; the plan was ultimately abandoned. A studio version of the composition, oil on canvas, c. 1745 to 1750, is Cleveland Museum of Art accession 1983.217, hanging in Gallery 217. Month and day are placeholders.
stops.campa: The basilica wants the subject and cannot keep paint on its walls, so the commission is for a design to be worked in tesserae. Batoni paints Peter kneeling and the demons letting go of the man they had been holding up, so that the real action of the picture is a withdrawal of support in mid-air. The mosaic is never finished and the project is abandoned. What survives of it is a studio canvas in oil, which hangs two centuries later in Gallery 217 of the Cleveland Museum of Art.
sources: Cleveland Museum of Art, object page 1983.217 (clevelandart.org/art/1983.217)
suggested_refs: Pompeo Batoni, The Fall of Simon Magus, Cleveland Museum of Art 1983.217, Gallery 217 (41.5085, -81.612)

stops.name: Nag Hammadi, the sealed jar
stops.date_confidence: A for the find, R for the attribution. Thirteen Coptic codices were dug up near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt in December 1945; Codex VI contains The Concept of Our Great Power, transmitted under no author's name. M. David Litwa in 2024 proposes it and the Declaration of Great Power as early second-century Simonian compositions from Alexandria or Egypt; that is a modern reconstruction, not an ancient claim, and the monograph was not directly consulted. The Mead volume of 1892 is A for existence, with its online text unreachable this pass. Day is a placeholder.
stops.campa: Peasants digging for fertilizer at the foot of a cliff in Upper Egypt open a sealed jar full of Coptic books. One of them, in the sixth codex, is called The Concept of Our Great Power, and it carries no author's name. G. R. S. Mead had attempted a rehabilitation of Simon from a Theosophical desk in London in 1892, with no manuscripts to do it with. Nearly eighty years after the jar came out of the ground, M. David Litwa argues that this text and a related one belong to a real second-century movement with its own literature, to be reconstructed from what it wrote rather than from what Irenaeus said about it.
sources: M. David Litwa, Simon of Samaria and the Simonians (2024), via secondary characterization
G. R. S. Mead, Simon Magus: An Essay on the Founder of Simonianism (London, 1892); online text unreachable, certificate error
suggested_refs: The Concept of Our Great Power, Nag Hammadi Codex VI,4
